items.question: What did building Google Now's personalized news-delivery infrastructure teach you about engineering performance?
items.object: Engineering and infrastructure for Google Now's personalized news delivery
items.answer: When I got to the team, they realized there was actually a lot to do in engineering, especially infrastructure. For example, if there was a new news story that they wanted to personalize and send to people using the app, I built a system that could push a newly published story to everyone's phones within four or five minutes. That taught me a lot about infrastructure. Once, we saw that sending a news item was slow—it took one hundred milliseconds—and everyone was asking why it was so slow. I looked at where the data was, and I found that one end was on the East Coast, while I was sending the data to the West Coast. Based on the speed of light, that amount of time was simply unavoidable; you could not make it faster. I learned a lot of engineering and end-to-end work.

items.question: How do you understand the significance of Geoffrey Hinton’s arrival at Google for its approach to AI?
items.object: Geoffrey Hinton’s arrival at Google and Google’s shift toward deep learning
items.answer: After Hinton arrived, Google placed a great deal of importance on AI. I remember that in those years our CEO also said Google was an AI company, because AI was at its core. The algorithm Larry Page and Sergey Brin created at the beginning also had AI as its goal: getting machines to help people understand what people wrote on the internet. So they had always valued AI. But after 2012, a new phase began: the deep-learning phase. They felt that if they did not invest in that direction, they would fall behind. So they acquired Geoffrey Hinton's company. From then on, deep learning became very important to Google, and its models increasingly became neural-network models.

items.question: How did you arrive at the idea of combining language-model training with supervised fine-tuning in “Semi-supervised Sequence Learning”?
items.object: The discovery behind “Semi-supervised Sequence Learning”
items.answer: We did not predict it from the beginning; it was not planned. We had originally been working on a technology called paragraph vector. At the time there was Word2vec, called word embeddings. Before LLMs, people used those things, and we wanted to make something better. I ran many experiments, and they all failed. But one day I ran an experiment and found that the result was very good, scoring higher than other papers. But when I wanted to reproduce it and rerun it, I could not reproduce the earlier result. So I thought there must be a bug somewhere, something had gone wrong. I dug into it for a while and discovered that when training the model, I had started from a checkpoint from another project. That other project was a language-model project, and I had started from there. So I discovered that if you first train a language model and then fine-tune it on supervised data, you can get a very good model. That was what we discovered, and we turned it into a paper. Previously those two things were separate; people had not thought of using language models for language understanding. Our idea was that combining a language model with fine-tuning could make a very good model. We were the first to put those two parts together.

items.question: Why do you see FLAN’s approach to instruction fine-tuning as important?
items.object: FLAN instruction fine-tuning
items.answer: Before FLAN, people used things like few-shot prompting with these models. If you wanted a model to do something, you first had to give it examples. For a math problem, you would give it a math problem and the answer, then provide several examples before asking it to do something. The FLAN paper said you do not actually need to give examples at inference time; it is enough to put these examples into the fine-tuning data. The model then learns that whatever question you give it, it has to provide an answer. I see a good side and a bad side. The good side is that you no longer need to provide those few-shot examples. But the bad side, which everyone knows now, is that if you ask it something it does not know, it will still pretend that it knows. This made a ChatGPT-like chatbot possible, because you can ask it questions directly.

items.question: How has Jeff Hinton’s brain-inspired approach to AI shaped your own research taste?

items.answer: I think my research taste came from Jeff Hinton and his group. Jeff Hinton believed that if we do AI, we should follow ideas from the brain.
